0.title: What Is Mine to Carry
0.essay:
Every day the world arrives at our door. A friend’s marriage is in trouble. A church on the other side of the country is splitting. A war fills the evening news, and an election abroad fills the morning feed. We hear about more need in a single day than our grandparents heard about in a year. What are we supposed to do with all of it?

Two kinds of weight

Some Christians feel they must act on everything they hear. A need reaches their ears, and at once it becomes their job. Others have learned to shrug. If it is not on their doorstep, it is not their business.

The Bible gives a better way. It distinguishes between what God has given me to carry and what I may care about. Some things are my responsibility: God has placed them in my hands, and he will ask me about them. A husband and father, for example, is answerable for whether his family opens the Bible together. Other things are my concern: I care, I pray, I may help where I can, but they are not mine to carry. Another family’s habits or the politics of a country far away matter, but they are in other hands, and finally in God’s.

Faithful and at rest

Learning the difference makes us more faithful where God has placed us, and lets us rest about what he has not. Beneath both stands Christ, who carried what was truly ours, our sin and its judgment, and who now holds together everything that is beyond us. Because he carries the world, we can carry our small portion.

The chapters

Two Circles; What Is Mine; What to Do with a Concern; When Concern Takes Over; “Not My Problem”; and Living It Out. The studies Control and Trust and Busy, Tired & Restless sit close to this one.

For reflection

Which do you lean towards: feeling responsible for everything you hear about, or treating little beyond your own life as your business? What is one situation on your mind today that you are unsure whether to carry or to leave?

1.title: Two Circles
1.essay:
Picture two circles, one drawn inside the other. The small inner circle holds what God has given you to carry. The large outer circle holds what you may care about. Both are real. But they are not the same, and much of our anxiety, and much of our neglect, comes from confusing them.

Burdens and loads

Paul puts two sentences close together in Galatians 6 that seem at first to contradict each other. “Bear one another’s burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ” (Galatians 6:2). Then, three verses later: “For each will have to bear his own load” (Galatians 6:5). Which is it? Do I carry other people’s weight, or only my own?

Paul uses two different words. The “burden” of verse 2 is a heavy weight, more than one person can manage: a sin that has caught someone, a grief, a crisis. When a brother or sister is crushed like that, we gather round and lift. The “load” of verse 5 is a different word, used for a pack or a soldier’s kit, the ordinary weight each person is expected to carry. No one else can carry my load for me. I will answer for my own life, my own work and my own obedience.

Stewards, not owners

From the beginning God gave human beings a particular place to tend. “The LORD God took the man and put him in the garden of Eden to work it and keep it” (Genesis 2:15). Adam was given a garden, with work to do and something to guard. That is the shape of a calling: a place, a task, and an account to give.

Paul says the same about the Christian life: “Only let each person lead the life that the Lord has assigned to him, and to which God has called him” (1 Corinthians 7:17). Assigned. God has placed each of us in a family, a town, a church, a job, with these people and not others. Paul even spoke of his own ministry as “the area of influence God assigned to us” (2 Corinthians 10:13). He had a field. He did not pretend to have every field.

Things too great for me

David, a king with real responsibilities, wrote one of the shortest psalms: “O LORD, my heart is not lifted up; my eyes are not raised too high; I do not occupy myself with things too great and too marvelous for me” (Psalm 131:1). He was not lazy or indifferent. He ruled a nation. But he knew there were things beyond his reach, and he did not make them his business. The result was not neglect but peace: “But I have calmed and quieted my soul, like a weaned child with its mother” (Psalm 131:2).

Moses drew a similar line: “The secret things belong to the LORD our God, but the things that are revealed belong to us and to our children forever” (Deuteronomy 29:29). The study Control and Trust works this verse out. Here notice only that some things “belong to us”. Many more do not.

Responsibility and concern

It helps to name the two circles plainly. Responsibility is what God has placed in my hands: where I have a role, some authority, and an account to give. If I neglect it, someone is wronged. Concern is what touches my heart but lies in someone else’s hands. I may pray, I may encourage, I may sometimes give or help. But I am not answerable for the outcome, and I am not required to act every time I think of it.

Both circles come from love. The inner circle is where love is most concentrated, because there God has trusted us with real people and real work. The outer circle is where love is spread wide in prayer and goodwill. A Christian with no outer circle has a small heart. A Christian who tries to turn the whole outer circle into the inner one will be crushed, and will often neglect the inner circle while he tries.

An example

A woman in her fifties carries a constant ache of guilt. Her prayer list runs to four pages. She feels personally responsible for a cousin’s failing marriage, a struggling church in another city, a friend’s wayward teenager and the refugees she sees on television. Meanwhile she has not had a proper conversation with her own husband for weeks. An older friend asks her a simple question: “Which of these has God actually put in your hands?” She goes quiet. Then she draws two circles on the back of an envelope. It is the beginning of a long lesson, and of a lighter heart.

For reflection

What is the difference between the “burden” of Galatians 6:2 and the “load” of Galatians 6:5? What would you put in your inner circle, and what in your outer one? Is there anything in your outer circle that you have been treating as if it were your responsibility? What would it mean for you to say, with David, that you do not occupy yourself with things too great for you?

2.title: What Is Mine
2.essay:
If the inner circle is what God has given me to carry, what is in it? For most Christians the answer is less dramatic than we expect. It is the people under our own roof, the work in front of us, the church we belong to, the place we live, and the neighbour God actually puts on our road.

The home

For most people the first callings are in the home. A husband is to love his wife “as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her” (Ephesians 5:25). Fathers are to bring their children up “in the discipline and instruction of the Lord” (Ephesians 6:4). Wives and mothers are called to love their husbands and children (Titus 2:4), and children owe honour to their parents. Paul is blunt: “if anyone does not provide for his relatives, and especially for members of his household, he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever” (1 Timothy 5:8).

This is where spiritual responsibility is most concrete. Moses told Israel’s parents that God’s words “shall be on your heart. You shall teach them diligently to your children, and shall talk of them when you sit in your house, and when you walk by the way” (Deuteronomy 6:6–7). Whether a family opens the Bible together is not the pastor’s responsibility, or the grandparents’, or the youth group’s. They may help. But God asks it of the father and mother in that home. Joshua could not decide for the whole nation, but he could say, “But as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD” (Joshua 24:15).

A single person or a widow has a household too, and relatives God has knitted into it. The point is simple: home is near, it is yours, and it comes first.

Work, church and city

Work is a calling too. “Whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord and not for men” (Colossians 3:23). The job I am paid for and the tasks I have agreed to do are mine. The rest of the company’s problems usually are not.

Church membership brings responsibilities: to worship, to serve with the gifts God has given, to love and pray for one another, to support those who lead. Elders carry a heavier share, for they keep watch over souls “as those who will have to give an account” (Hebrews 13:17).

Citizenship is a calling as well. God told the exiles in Babylon, “seek the welfare of the city where I have sent you into exile, and pray to the LORD on its behalf” (Jeremiah 29:7). We obey lawful authorities, pay taxes and do good to the place we live. For those called to public office, politics is part of the inner circle.

The neighbour on my road

When a lawyer asked Jesus, “And who is my neighbor?” (Luke 10:29), Jesus told of a man beaten and left half dead. A Samaritan “came to where he was, and when he saw him, he had compassion” (Luke 10:33). The Samaritan did not set out to solve the problem of robbery on every road in Judea. He met one man on his own road and did what he could for him (Luke 10:34–35).

The parable makes its main point plainly. Jesus turns the question round: not “Who qualifies as my neighbour?” but which of the three “proved to be a neighbor” (Luke 10:36). Love does not limit itself by labels. But notice too that it was concrete and near. The neighbour God puts in front of me is part of my inner circle for as long as he is there. “So then, as we have opportunity, let us do good to everyone” (Galatians 6:10). Opportunity is the word. Not every need in the world, but the ones God brings across my path.

Faithful in a little

None of this sounds very grand. That is the point. Jesus said, “One who is faithful in a very little is also faithful in much” (Luke 16:10). Paul says, “it is required of stewards that they be found faithful” (1 Corinthians 4:2). Not successful, not famous, not involved in everything: faithful. The master in the parable says, “You have been faithful over a little; I will set you over much” (Matthew 25:21).

Even on the cross, carrying the sin of the world, Jesus saw his mother standing nearby and gave her into the care of the disciple he loved: “Behold, your mother!” And “from that hour the disciple took her to his own home” (John 19:27). The Saviour of the world did not forget the small, near duty of a son.

An example

A father of three young children serves on two church committees and leads a midweek group. He is respected and busy. One evening his eight-year-old asks why they never read the Bible at home like her friend’s family does. It stings. He resigns from one committee, and the next night, after dinner, he reads a short passage from Mark and prays for two minutes. It is awkward at first. Months later it is the part of the day the children remind him about.

For reflection

Name the callings God has given you: home, work, church, city. Which of them have you been neglecting while you attended to things further away? Who is the neighbour God has put on your road this week? What small, faithful thing could you do in your inner circle today?

3.title: What to Do with a Concern
3.essay:
So what do we do with everything in the outer circle? The family down the road whose children have drifted from church. The congregation across the country in turmoil. The famine, the war, the election. Scripture does not tell us to ignore these things. It shows us what to do with them: pray, speak where it is fitting, give where we are able, and then leave them with God.

First, pray

Prayer is the one thing we can do for every concern, however far away. Paul writes, “First of all, then, I urge that supplications, prayers, intercessions, and thanksgivings be made for all people, for kings and all who are in high positions” (1 Timothy 2:1–2). Christians in Ephesus had no vote in Rome and no say over Nero’s policies. But they could pray for him, and Paul calls that “first of all”.

Prayer is not a consolation prize. It brings the concern to the one who holds it. Samuel said to Israel, “far be it from me that I should sin against the LORD by ceasing to pray for you” (1 Samuel 12:23).

Nehemiah before he had authority

Nehemiah is a fine example. He was a servant in the Persian court, the king’s cupbearer, hundreds of miles from Jerusalem. When he heard that the city’s wall was broken down and its people in disgrace, he did not hire a caravan the next morning. “As soon as I heard these words I sat down and wept and mourned for days, and I continued fasting and praying before the God of heaven” (Nehemiah 1:4).

His prayer closed with a request for one specific opening: “give success to your servant today, and grant him mercy in the sight of this man” (Nehemiah 1:11). Then he waited, about four months, until the king himself noticed his sad face and asked, “What are you requesting?” Nehemiah tells us, “So I prayed to the God of heaven. And I said to the king…” (Nehemiah 2:4–5). Only then did the concern become his commission, with letters and timber and authority. Until then his part was to grieve, pray and be ready.

Speak a word, give a gift

Sometimes a concern allows a word. A friend whose family no longer opens the Bible together might welcome encouragement, perhaps a book or an invitation. Speak it once, kindly and clearly, and then trust God with it. You are not appointed to check every week. You are not that family’s head; someone else is, and God will deal with him.

Sometimes a concern allows a gift. We cannot fly to every disaster, but we can give to those who are there, as the Greek churches gave for poor believers in Jerusalem they would never meet. Paul felt “the daily pressure on me of my anxiety for all the churches” (2 Corinthians 11:28), yet he did not try to be everywhere. He prayed, wrote, sent co-workers and trusted the Spirit and the local elders.

Politics and the news

Christians differ about how far believers should engage in politics. Some urge every believer to be an activist. Others say the church should keep out of politics altogether and concentrate on the gospel.

This commentary’s view: citizenship is a real calling, so Christians should pray for those in authority, obey just laws, vote thoughtfully where they can, and speak up for the vulnerable, and some are called to serve in public life. But the church’s pulpit should not endorse parties, and faithful Christians may disagree on many policy questions. For most believers, the politics of other nations, and much of their own, belongs in the outer circle: something to pray about and care about, not something to be consumed by. “Fret not yourself because of evildoers” (Psalm 37:1). “Fret not yourself; it tends only to evil” (Psalm 37:8). The study The Christian & the World says more about Christians and politics.

Then leave it with God

The last step is the hardest: leave it. “Do not be anxious about anything, but in everything by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known to God” (Philippians 4:6). The promise that follows does not say God will fix everything at once. It says, “the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus” (Philippians 4:7). Peter adds, “casting all your anxieties on him, because he cares for you” (1 Peter 5:7).

The one we leave it with is not distant. “The king’s heart is a stream of water in the hand of the LORD; he turns it wherever he will” (Proverbs 21:1). “He removes kings and sets up kings” (Daniel 2:21). The far-off concern is not unattended. It is in better hands than ours.

An example

A woman learns that a family she knows from a previous church has stopped attending anywhere. She lies awake composing long messages. Instead, she prays for them by name for a week, then sends a short, warm note saying she misses them and would love to have them for a meal. They come once. They do not come back to church. She keeps praying, now once a week, and she has learned to sleep.

For reflection

Which concerns in your outer circle do you most need to turn into prayer? What can you learn from Nehemiah’s months of praying before he could act? Is there one word you should speak, or one gift you should give, and then leave? How does Proverbs 21:1 change the way you hear the news?

4.title: When Concern Takes Over
4.essay:
Some people cannot hear of a need without feeling that it is now their job. They are often the kindest people in a church, and the most tired. But when concern takes over, something has gone wrong, not only in the diary but in the heart.

The over-responsible heart

The over-responsible heart has several faces. There is anxiety: the mind cannot let go, and lies awake over problems it can do nothing about. There is control: if I do not hold it together, it will fall apart. There is a hidden pride: I am needed, I am indispensable, they cannot manage without me. And there is the wish to play saviour: to be the one who rescues, fixes and makes everything right.

The study Control and Trust traces the craving for control back to the garden and shows how Christ frees us from it. This chapter looks at something narrower: what happens when we take on loads God never gave us. Scripture names the danger in a single word, the “meddler” (1 Peter 4:15), and Proverbs gives a vivid picture: “Whoever meddles in a quarrel not his own is like one who takes a passing dog by the ears” (Proverbs 26:17). You will be bitten.

Moses and Jethro

Moses sat from morning till evening judging every dispute among Israel. His father-in-law watched and said, “What you are doing is not good. You and the people with you will certainly wear yourselves out, for the thing is too heavy for you. You are not able to do it alone” (Exodus 18:17–18). Jethro’s advice was to share it: let able, God-fearing men decide the small matters, “and they will bear the burden with you” (Exodus 18:22).

The study Busy, Tired & Restless looks at this as a lesson about weariness. Notice also what it says about responsibility. Moses was trying to carry other people’s callings. There were capable men in Israel whom God meant to use, and as long as Moses did everything, they did nothing. The over-responsible person often robs others of their own God-given work.

Martha’s many things

Martha had Jesus in her house and was “distracted with much serving” (Luke 10:40). Jesus said, “Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things, but one thing is necessary” (Luke 10:41–42). Martha was not wrong to serve. She was wrong to think everything was up to her, and wrong to want to manage her sister’s choices too.

Jesus moved on

The most freeing example is Jesus himself. After a day of healing in Capernaum he rose before dawn to pray. The disciples found him and said, “Everyone is looking for you.” He answered, “Let us go on to the next towns, that I may preach there also, for that is why I came out” (Mark 1:37–38). There were still sick people in Capernaum. He had the power to heal every one of them. Yet he left, because the Father had given him a particular work, and it was not to heal everyone everywhere.

He also declined tasks that were not his. A man in the crowd said, “Teacher, tell my brother to divide the inheritance with me.” Jesus answered, “Man, who made me a judge or arbitrator over you?” (Luke 12:13–14). Jesus cared about the greed beneath it, but settling it was not his calling. If the Son of God could say, “That is not mine to decide,” so can we.

At the end of his ministry, with countless needs still unmet in Israel, he could say to the Father, “I glorified you on earth, having accomplished the work that you gave me to do” (John 17:4). Not every work, but the work you gave me.

What is that to you?

After the resurrection, Jesus told Peter how he would die. Peter looked at John and asked, “Lord, what about this man?” Jesus said, “If it is my will that he remain until I come, what is that to you? You follow me!” (John 21:21–22). It is a gentle rebuke, and a great relief. Peter’s path was Peter’s. John’s was John’s. Jesus was Lord of both.

Much of our over-concern is Peter’s question again: what about that family, that church, that country? Often the answer is the same: “What is that to you? You follow me.”

An example

A deacon in a small church is the person everyone calls. He drives people to hospital, fixes the boiler, chases unpaid bills and visits every newcomer. He feels guilty when he says no, so he never does. After two years his wife says she hardly sees him, and his own prayer life has gone quiet. The elders sit down with him and, like Jethro, divide the work among four others. He finds, to his surprise, that the others are glad to be asked, and that the church does not collapse when he goes on holiday.

If over-concern has become constant anxiety that will not lift, with sleeplessness, dread or exhaustion, tell your pastor and seek out a biblical counsellor, through your church, or if your church has none, through a biblical counselling organisation (for example ACBC or CCEF in the US, Biblical Counselling UK in Britain). A good biblical counsellor will ask you to have a medical check-up, because anxiety can have physical causes, and will then help you work through it from God’s Word. If the doctor recommends treatment, receiving it is no failure of faith.

For reflection

Which face of the over-responsible heart do you recognise in yourself: anxiety, control, pride or playing saviour? Is there work you are doing that God means others to do? Where do you need to hear Jesus say, “What is that to you? You follow me”? How does it help that Jesus left needs unmet in Capernaum?

5.title: “Not My Problem”
5.essay:
There is a ditch on the other side of the road. Having learned that not everything is ours, we can slide into treating almost nothing as ours. “It’s not my problem” can be wisdom. It can also be the oldest excuse in the world.

Am I my brother’s keeper?

The first time the phrase appears, it is on the lips of a murderer. God asked Cain, “Where is Abel your brother?” Cain answered, “I do not know; am I my brother’s keeper?” (Genesis 4:9). The answer God expected was obvious. Abel was his brother. Cain had not merely failed to protect him; he had killed him. But the question has echoed ever since as the voice of a heart that wants no claims on it. Some things are our business because God has bound us to people, and we cannot shrug them off.

The priest and the Levite

In Jesus’ parable, a priest came down the road, saw the wounded man, “and when he saw him he passed by on the other side.” A Levite did the same (Luke 10:31–32). They may have had reasons: ritual purity, fear of robbers, an appointment. But the man was in front of them, half dead, and they had the means to help. The need was near, it was serious, and they could do something. In that moment it was theirs.

This is where the two circles touch. A man in a distant land is in my outer circle. The same man lying on my road has stepped into my inner one. Nearness changes things.

We did not know

Proverbs closes the door on a common excuse. “Rescue those who are being taken away to death; hold back those who are stumbling to the slaughter. If you say, ‘Behold, we did not know this,’ does not he who weighs the heart perceive it?” (Proverbs 24:11–12). Sometimes we do not know. But sometimes we have made sure not to know, because knowing would make demands of us. God sees the difference.

John asks the same question in a gentler key: “if anyone has the world’s goods and sees his brother in need, yet closes his heart against him, how does God’s love abide in him?” (1 John 3:17). Proverbs adds, “Do not withhold good from those to whom it is due, when it is in your power to do it” (Proverbs 3:27).

For such a time as this

Esther is the clearest picture of a concern becoming a responsibility. She was queen, but she could not approach the king unbidden without risking death. Mordecai answered her: “Do not think to yourself that in the king’s palace you will escape any more than all the other Jews” (Esther 4:13). And then: “For if you keep silent at this time, relief and deliverance will rise for the Jews from another place, but you and your father’s house will perish. And who knows whether you have not come to the kingdom for such a time as this?” (Esther 4:14).

Notice both sides. Mordecai was sure that God would deliver his people one way or another; the rescue did not depend on Esther. Yet her position had put her where she could act, and to keep silent would be faithless. She called for fasting and went in: “if I perish, I perish” (Esther 4:16).

When a concern becomes mine

How can we tell when something in the outer circle has moved into the inner one? Scripture gives no formula, but it gives several signs.

Authority. Has God given me a role here? A parent, a manager, an elder, a teacher, a carer: where I hold authority, the matter is mine. Esther’s crown made her people’s danger her business.

Nearness. Is it on my road? The wounded man in front of me, the lonely neighbour next door, the colleague whose distress I see every day.

Ability. Can I actually do something that would help? “In your power to do it”, says Proverbs. A concern I cannot affect, except by prayer, usually stays a concern.

Being asked or called. Has someone come to me? Has the church asked me to serve? Paul was kept from preaching in Asia, then saw a man of Macedonia saying, “Come over to Macedonia and help us” (Acts 16:9), and concluded that God had called them there. A clear request or an open door can mark a concern becoming a commission, as it did for Nehemiah.

The counsel of others. Wise friends, a spouse, the elders of the church can often see what we cannot: both what we are neglecting and what we should put down.

None of these alone decides it. When several point the same way, God is likely handing you something to carry.

An example

A man manages a small team at work. He hears that one of his staff is being mocked and excluded by two others. For weeks he tells himself it is a personal matter and not his business. Then he reads Proverbs 24 and realises that he is the one person with the authority to stop it. He speaks to the two staff members, sets clear expectations, and checks on the one who has been mistreated. It was his to do all along.

For reflection

When have you said, in effect, “Am I my brother’s keeper?” Is there a need near you that you have been making sure not to know about? Which of the five signs (authority, nearness, ability, being asked, counsel) applies to a situation you are facing now? Whom could you ask for counsel about it?

6.title: Living It Out
6.essay:
Telling responsibility from concern is not a skill we learn once. We practise it every day, as news arrives, messages come in and people tell us their troubles. This last chapter offers some simple habits, and then lifts our eyes to the one who makes it possible to carry our small portion in peace.

Three questions

When something new lands on your heart, ask three questions. First: Is this mine to carry? Is it in my home, my work, my church, my road, or has God given me authority or a clear call here? If so, act, and do it faithfully. Second: Is this mine to pray about? Almost always, yes. Pray, perhaps speak once, perhaps give, and then let it go. Third: Is this simply not mine? Some things are other people’s business, or idle curiosity, or a quarrel we have no part in. Leave those altogether.

It can help to say the answer aloud: “Lord, this is mine; help me do it.” Or, “Lord, this is yours; I give it to you.” Some find it helps to keep two lists: what I must do this week, and what I am praying about.

The news and the feed

Our great-grandparents heard about far-off disasters weeks later, in a newspaper, if at all. We hear about every one of them within minutes, many times over, with pictures, and with a stream of opinion designed to make us angry or afraid. We were not made to carry the whole world’s troubles every hour.

Knowing what is happening helps us pray and act wisely as citizens. But we may need limits. Read or watch the news once a day, not all day. Choose sources that inform rather than inflame. Notice when scrolling has turned to fretting, and stop. Turn the headlines into prayer, and then close the screen. “Fret not yourself; it tends only to evil” (Psalm 37:8). The study Technology & the Christian Mind says more about our screens.

Social media adds a trap: the feeling that we must have an opinion on everything and say it at once. We do not. Most controversies are not ours to settle.

A weekly look at the circles

Once a week, perhaps on the Lord’s Day, look over your two circles. In the inner one: How are things at home? Have we opened the Bible together? Is there a neighbour I have neglected, a duty at work or church I have let slide? In the outer one: What am I praying about? Has anything here become mine, or have I been carrying what is not? Then rest. The week’s unfinished business is in God’s hands.

The one who carried what was ours

Underneath all this lies the gospel. There was one load that was truly ours, and that we could never carry: our sin and the judgment it deserves. Christ carried it. “Surely he has borne our griefs and carried our sorrows… and the LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all” (Isaiah 53:4–6). “He himself bore our sins in his body on the tree” (1 Peter 2:24). The heaviest weight in our lives has been lifted, by the only one strong enough to bear it.

That changes how we carry everything else. We do not work in our inner circle to earn God’s favour. We already have it. We are faithful because we are loved. And because the great load is gone, Jesus can offer us a different yoke: “Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest… For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light” (Matthew 11:28–30).

The one who holds what is beyond us

And what of the outer circle, the wars, the elections, the distant churches, the families we cannot reach? Christ holds that too. “He is before all things, and in him all things hold together” (Colossians 1:17). He “upholds the universe by the word of his power” (Hebrews 1:3). Isaiah foresaw a child of whom it is said, “the government shall be upon his shoulder” (Isaiah 9:6). The government of the world is not on your shoulders. It is on his, and his shoulders are not weary.

So we can be faithful in our small portion and rest about the rest. The father reading Mark with his children, the woman praying for a family she cannot reach, the citizen who votes and prays and then sleeps: each is doing what a creature should do, under a King who reigns over all. “In peace I will both lie down and sleep; for you alone, O LORD, make me dwell in safety” (Psalm 4:8).

An example

A retired man used to begin every day with an hour of news and end it with another, and went to bed angry about countries he would never visit. Now he reads the news once, after he has read his Bible. He keeps a short list of places and people he prays for, and gives monthly to a mission working in one of them. He spends the hour he saved with his grandson, who lives nearby and has had a hard year. He still cares about the world. He has stopped trying to carry it.

For reflection

Which of the three questions do you most need to ask this week? What one change could you make in how you take in news or social media? How does it help to know that the government of the world is on Christ’s shoulders, not yours? What is your small portion today, and how will you be faithful in it?
